html:
The Tunica were a people of the lower Mississippi valley, in what is now western Mississippi, eastern Arkansas and Louisiana. Their language, Tunica, is an isolate, related to no other known language.

They farmed maize, beans and squash, and were heirs to the Mississippian world of mound towns. They were also known as traders, above all of salt, which they made by boiling down spring water. The Hernando de Soto expedition passed through their region in 1541.

In the late 1600s they moved south down the river and became close allies of the French in Louisiana, part of New France. They fought on the French side against the Natchez, who attacked their village in 1731. They later settled near Marksville, Louisiana, together with the Biloxi. Goods from their graves of the 1700s, looted in the 1960s and later returned to the tribe, are known as the Tunica Treasure. Today their descendants form the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana. Their neighbours included the Houma and Choctaw.
sum: The Tunica were a people of the lower Mississippi valley, in what is now western Mississippi, eastern Arkansas and Louisiana. Their language, Tunica, is an isolate, related to no other known language.
